extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of theology and political philosophy; clergy and statesmen interested in church–state authority
extracted.subtask_description: A historical/theological argument assessing the proper distribution of ecclesiastical and civil powers — especially whether Christian sovereigns may baptize, consecrate, and exercise supreme ecclesiastical authority, and whether the Pope holds universal jurisdiction or infallibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christian Kings' power to baptize and consecrate
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian Kings have power to Baptize, to Administer the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper, and to Consecrate both Temples and Pastors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: This power derives from the Right of his Office (analogous to a king lecturing or sitting in judgment), not from a special ecclesiastical ceremony; sovereigns often do not perform these rites themselves because the charge of government consumes their time (examples: our Saviour and S. Paul baptized few themselves). The author intends to show both why they do not commonly do it and how they are capable of it without ordinary imposition of hands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imposition of hands as public designation (purpose and examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imposition of Hands is an ancient public ceremony used to designate and make certain the person or thing intended in blessing, sacrifice, consecration, condemnation, or prayer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biblical and historical examples cited: Jacob laying hands on Ephraim and Manasseh; Aaron laying hands on the bullock and ram; Moses ordaining Joshua by laying on hands; consecration of Levites; congregation laying hands on blasphemer; Aaron lifting up his hand to bless the people. Among Christians: Apostles and Presbyters laid hands on ordained pastors and on the seven Deacons (Acts 6:6); Peter and John laid hands on converts in Samaria (Acts 8:17). The ceremony's practical function is visual designation ('to the Eye') rather than merely verbal appointment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imposition of hands unnecessary if office already designates
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a person is already instituted to power (e.g., the sovereign's office or by prior teaching authority), the ceremonial imposition of hands is not necessary to authorize pastoral functions; Baptism can be sufficient to authorize right preaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: If someone already had the power of teaching, their baptism would not give a new power but would cause them to preach true doctrine; hence imposition of hands was a ceremony of designation rather than the exclusive source of ministerial authority. Citation: Paul's practice and Timothy's case (1 Tim. 4.14; 2 Tim. 1:6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil sovereign (if Christian) is head of the church in his dominions
rubrics_metrics.description: A civil sovereign who is a Christian is the head of the Church within his own dominions and holds supreme power over external actions in both policy and religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: he may make laws for religious governance of his subjects; he may appoint judges and interpreters of canonical scripture for his realm; he may give force to excommunications by civil punishment; he may commit religious government to the Pope or to assemblies but retains the civil right to discharge or modify such delegations. The author treats State and Church as the same body of men in a Christian commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign's power to appoint ecclesiastical structures and provide maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: The sovereign may commit care of religion to a supreme pastor or assembly of pastors, give titles (bishops, archbishops, priests, presbyters), and make laws for their maintenance (tithes or other means), provided he acts from sincere conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the sovereign delegates, the delegated church authority functions by Jure Civili (civil right) in that dominion and is subordinate to the sovereign; such delegated officers can be discharged by the sovereign for the good of his subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastors' office limited to teaching and persuasion, not coercive governance
rubrics_metrics.description: The calling of pastors is to teach and persuade, not to govern men by command; they are not 'masters of families' with coercive civil power unless such power is annexed by the civil sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: pastoral authority without civil sovereignty lacks power to impose civil penalties; pastors should rely on argument rather than command, and their 'laws' are not civil laws unless backed by the sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present established government should be maintained and is absolute for obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: All governments which men are bound to obey are simple and absolute; therefore, where any one form of government (monarchy, aristocracy, democracy) is already established, it ought to be preferred and maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: changing established government contravenes natural and divine positive law; the distinction drawn is between sovereigns (those with absolute power) and pastors, who have different functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'Thou art Peter' (Matt. 16) — foundation is confession, not Petrine person
rubrics_metrics.description: The words 'Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church' refer to the foundational article of faith (Peter's confession that Jesus is the Christ), not to a grant of universal personal primacy to Peter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linguistic point: original allusion to Simon's name (Cephas/Petrus = stone) explains the phrasing; parallel passages (e.g., Matthew 18:18) and the context show the power belongs to supreme pastors generally and is tied to the office of teaching rather than to one individual's worldly jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Antichrist for identifying the Antichrist
rubrics_metrics.description: Antichrist (in proper signification) has two essential marks: (1) denies Jesus is the Christ; (2) professes himself to be the Christ (i.e., claims to be Christ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore, someone who neither denies Christ nor claims to be Christ (e.g., the Pope, who professes Christ) does not meet the proper scriptural definition of Antichrist; the author distinguishes between 'an Antichrist' (many false christs) and 'the Antichrist' (one special person).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural texts cited for papal infallibility are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The scriptural passages Bellarmine cites (Luke 22:31–32; Matthew 16:18–19; John 21:15–17; Exodus 28:30; John 16:13) do not establish papal infallibility or universal jurisdiction in the dominions of other princes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific critiques: Luke 22 is about Peter's faith being preserved and a charge to strengthen brethren (not worldly jurisdiction); Matthew 16 refers to the confession as foundation; John 21 commands feeding sheep (teaching) not lawmaking; Exodus 28's Urim and Thummim gave 'evidence and truth' to the High Priest in Israel but, in historical practice, such functions attached to the civil sovereign of Israel; John 16's promise of the Spirit leading into truth pertains at most to truths necessary for salvation and would not confer universal temporal jurisdiction over other princes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between law and counsel (Acts 15 as counsel, not law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Law is distinguished from counsel by its motive: a law's reason is taken from the design and benefit of the prescriber, whereas counsel's reason is taken from the design and benefit of the recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application: Acts 15's decisions ('It hath seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden...') are counsel aimed at the benefit of converted Gentiles (salvation) rather than legislative commands binding by sovereign jurisdiction. Hence apostolic decrees of this kind are advisory, not universal civil law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative and punitive powers belong to civil sovereigns, not solely to bishops
rubrics_metrics.description: Places cited for papal legislative power (Deut. 17:12; Matthew 16; John 20:21; Romans 13; 1 Cor. 4:21) either concern the civil sovereign in Israel or are misread when applied to a universal papal legislative authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: Deut. 17 pertains to the High Priest as civil sovereign in Israel; Matthew 16 and similar texts are better read as conferring teaching authority (or applicable within the bounds of civil sovereignty); Romans 13 supports subjection to 'higher powers' (civil rulers), making double subjection (to both sovereign and Pope) impossible. Punishments like death, imprisonment, fines are civil instruments not inherent to ecclesiastical censures except where the civil sovereign enforces them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of excommunication versus civil punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Excommunication, in its own nature, is not a civil punishment but a denouncing of punishment (a spiritual separation) whose full punitive execution is reserved for Christ at judgment unless supported by civil enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because excommunication without civil backing is 'only a leaving of their company' (akin to treating someone as a heathen), its force depends on civil laws and punishments to humble obstinate persons; otherwise it remains a spiritual denunciation rather than a temporal penalty.
